meta.title: Lock Screen Verse for Grief: Scripture for Each Season of Loss
meta.description: A lock screen verse for grief should fit where you are. 12 KJV verses for the first weeks, the long middle and later, plus how to keep their photo in place.

sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **FaithWall** keeps the verses you choose on your iPhone lock screen, as a wallpaper applied by an Apple Shortcut or a widget that rotates them, so Scripture is already there when grief hits in the middle of an ordinary day. The best **lock screen verse for grief** sits with the sorrow instead of explaining it: start with Psalm 34:18 or Matthew 5:4.

sections.text: Grief keeps no schedule. It catches you in the grocery line, at a red light, when their name surfaces in your contacts. FaithWall is built for those moments: you choose the verses, and they wait on the screen you reach for anyway. Choosing a **lock screen verse for grief** is less about the most beautiful line in the Bible than the one you can bear to read today. Below are 12 King James verses sorted by the season of loss they fit, a setup that keeps their photo where it is, and two verses worth saving for later. The [daily Scripture lock screen guide](/daily-scripture-lock-screen) covers the wider picture.
Why should a grief verse change with the season?

Because grief changes, and a verse that comforts in month six can sting in week one. Early grief usually needs permission to weep. The long middle needs proof you are not alone. Hope lands best once the first numbness lifts. Matching verse to season keeps Scripture honest about where you are.
The Psalms model this order. Psalm 13 opens with "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord?" and only reaches "I will sing unto the Lord" in its sixth and final verse. The lament comes first.
How do you set a grief verse without replacing their photo?

Use a lock-screen widget instead of a new wallpaper. On iOS 16 or later, widgets sit under the clock on any wallpaper, including a personal photo. The photo of the person you miss stays put, with the verse just below the time.

sections.text: A widget is a small space, so our rule of thumb is to keep verses over about 20 words for the full-screen wallpaper, which can use your own photo as its background. Comparing tools first? Here are the [lock-screen Bible verse apps side by side](/best-bible-verse-lock-screen-apps).

sections.text: 12 lock screen verses for grief, by season
All 12 are whole KJV verses, with word counts taken from the King James text behind this site's verse tools. Pick two or three from the season you're in, not all four.
The first weeks: verses that let you weep

items: John 11:35 (2 words) — "Jesus wept." He wept on the way to his friend's tomb, already knowing he would raise him.
Psalm 56:8 (17 words) — "Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?"
Psalm 13:1 (19 words) — "How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?"
Psalm 62:8 (21 words) — "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah."

sections.text: The long middle: verses that say you are not alone

items: Matthew 5:4 (10 words) — "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted."
Psalm 147:3 (11 words) — "He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."
Psalm 46:1 (12 words) — "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."
Psalm 23:4 (30 words) — "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

sections.text: Psalm 23 has its own [wallpaper setup guide](/blog/psalm-23-wallpaper-iphone) if you want the whole psalm in view. If fear has tangled itself into the grief, the [lock screen verses for anxiety](/blog/lock-screen-verses-for-anxiety) list goes there.
Later: verses that hold the hope

items: Lamentations 3:23 (9 words) — "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." It sits in a book of laments over a ruined city.
Psalm 30:5 (24 words) — "For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning."
1 Thessalonians 4:13 (26 words) — "But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope."

Revelation 21:4 (35 words) — "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."

sections.text: Notice what 1 Thessalonians 4:13 doesn't say. Paul never tells the church to stop sorrowing, only not to sorrow "as others which have no hope." Grief and hope share one sentence.

sections.content: **A verse you have to go looking for is one you won't find on the hardest days.** Grief drains the energy it takes to open a Bible app. The lock screen asks for nothing: you pick up the phone to check the time, and the verse is already there.

sections.text: Which verses should you hold back for now?

Romans 8:28 and Jeremiah 29:11 are true, and both are in our wallpaper gallery. In the first weeks of a loss, though, they tend to read as an explanation, as if the death were part of a plan you should already feel good about. Our call: save them for later, when you can hear them as promises.

Job's friends got the first week right. They sat on the ground with him seven days and seven nights, "and none spake a word unto him" (Job 2:13). The trouble started when they began explaining. Choosing a verse for a grieving friend? Romans 12:15 asks you to "weep with them that weep," not to fix it.
Where this gets hard: the verse that arrives on the wrong day

A random verse-of-the-day feed doesn't know what happened to you this week, so "Rejoice evermore" can land on the morning of the funeral. And a wallpaper you set by hand in week one still shows a lament in month six, because changing it means making and setting a new image when you have the least energy for it.

**FaithWall fixes both halves.** You chose every verse, so nothing random shows up, and swapping the set as the season turns takes a minute, not an image editor. Keep it on once a day: hourly rotation turns grief verses into a feed, while one verse a day is something to carry from morning to night.
The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
When is it more than grief?

Most grief softens on its own timeline, even when it never fully leaves. Some doesn't. When a loss still stops ordinary life a year or more later, it may be prolonged grief disorder, which the American Psychiatric Association added to its diagnostic manual in 2022.

sections.label: of adults bereaved by a natural death develop prolonged grief disorder
sections.description: Per a meta-analysis by Lundorff and colleagues in the Journal of Affective Disorders, pooling 14 studies: roughly one grieving adult in ten.

sections.text: If that sounds like you or someone you love, tell your pastor and talk to a doctor. A verse on the lock screen keeps you company in grief; it doesn't treat it. The best **lock screen verse for grief** is the one that keeps you honest with God while other people help carry the weight.
